title: Injury Time
desc: Rule loopholes, protest moments & records that will never be broken

questions.q: In 1994, Barbados needed to score an own goal to advance in a football tournament. Did they actually do it?
questions.a: Yes — due to a bizarre 'golden goal counts double' rule, they deliberately scored against themselves to force extra time, then won

questions.q: Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points in one NBA game. What's remarkable about the evidence?
questions.a: No complete video recording exists — only audio of the final minutes and a few photographs

questions.q: The 'Miracle of Istanbul' refers to which football match?
questions.a: 2005 Champions League Final — Liverpool came back from 3-0 down at half-time against AC Milan to win on penalties

questions.q: In tennis, what is a 'bagel' and a 'breadstick'?
questions.a: A bagel is winning a set 6-0, a breadstick is winning 6-1 (the 1 looks like a breadstick)

questions.q: Which Olympic sport was once judged partly on artistic impression alongside athletic performance — and still is?
questions.a: Figure skating, gymnastics, diving, synchronised swimming — all retain artistic/execution scores

questions.q: Why was the back-pass rule introduced in football in 1992?
questions.a: The 1990 World Cup was so boring — teams kept passing back to the keeper to waste time — that FIFA banned goalkeepers from handling deliberate back-passes

questions.q: In horse racing, who or what is 'Frankel' and why is he significant?
questions.a: An unbeaten British racehorse — 14 wins from 14 races (2010-2012), considered by many the greatest flat racehorse ever

questions.q: Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists on the podium at the 1968 Olympics. What happened to the third man on the podium?
questions.a: Peter Norman (silver, Australia) wore an Olympic Project for Human Rights badge in solidarity — he was ostracised by Australian athletics and never selected again

questions.q: What is the 'Duckworth-Lewis-Stern' method in cricket?
questions.a: A mathematical formula for resetting targets in rain-interrupted limited-overs matches — based on remaining resources (wickets and overs)

questions.q: The longest tennis match in history lasted over 11 hours across three days. Who played?
questions.a: John Isner vs Nicolas Mahut at Wimbledon 2010 — final score 70-68 in the fifth set
